cases.title: Bosnia 2018 Fuel Road Toll and Excise Rise
cases.place: Sarajevo, Tuzla, Banja Luka and Zenica, Bosnia and Herzegovina
cases.point: Sarajevo, one of the cities where roads were blocked in June 2018 (the tax was national)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Its €553 million aid deal listed passing the law as a key condition, and it froze further payments when the law failed (Reuters). On 9 February 2018 it released SDR 63.4 million (€74.6 million), noting the recent rise in fuel excise rates.

lenders.name: EBRD
lenders.role: Approved €220 million for infrastructure and another €250 million in loans, held up until the law passed; it treats road-toll money as a safeguard for debt repayment (Reuters).

lenders.name: European Commission
lenders.role: Made its €250 million of infrastructure loans conditional on the law (Reuters).

cases.conditions: Pass the changes to the excise law. Parliament passed them 22 to 20 on 15 December 2017, which Reuters said unlocked about €1 billion from the IMF, the EU and other lenders. The changes raised the road toll by 0.15 marks per litre of fuel and raised excise on biofuel, from 1 February 2018 (Eurofast, Reuters).
cases.community: Analyst Faruk Hadzic told N1 in June 2018 that world prices had risen by more than 0.50 marks a litre, that the price should now stand at 2.36 marks, that the tax rise was the trigger, and that distributors used the moment to raise prices further. He said higher fuel costs pushed up food and other goods. Protesters said an acceptable price was 1.50 to 1.70 marks. Foreign trade minister Mirko Šarović named the excise rise and world fuel prices as causes, and said more than 100 million marks from excise had reached the joint state account (N1).
cases.outcome: Transport companies led road blockades in Tuzla, Banja Luka, Sarajevo and Zenica and said they would mobilise daily. The Republika Srpska trade ministry announced a price drop, and some stations cut prices by 0.05 marks (N1).

cases.confidence_note: The condition is stated by Reuters and the law's passage is noted by the IMF. The harm shown is higher prices and road blockades; no count of households who lost income was found. The June 2018 price also reflected world oil prices, and the analyst said distributors added to it, so the tax was one cause. Reuters describes the excise rise as covering biofuel; the IMF and N1 speak of fuel excise.

lvwhy.tax: Road toll on fuel raised by 0.15 marks per litre to meet the loan condition.
lvwhy.prices: Pump prices and, by one analyst's account, food prices rose.

cases.suppression: Ten days into the late-2014 operation the energy minister said police had arrested or reported hundreds of people, mainly business owners, and 31 distribution workers (Top Channel). RAI-SEE reports hundreds arrested across the country for not paying bills. Citizens Channel gives two counts for the period to 2018: 91 arrested in one passage and 491 in another, from Roma and Egyptian activists; both add 71 detained, 1,079 investigated and 385 wanted.
cases.title: Albania Electricity Debt Arrests Under the Power Reform
cases.point: Tirana, seat of the government that ran the national operation; arrests took place across the country

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Approved the US$150 million Power Recovery Project on 29 September 2014, including support for power sector reforms; it says OShEE should gain from better billing and collection.

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: 36-month Extended Fund Facility approved 28 February 2014. In May 2014 its mission called for urgent reforms to improve collections and reduce theft; in November 2014 it listed curbs on electricity theft in the reform plan; in March 2015 it said the reform, developed in consultation with the World Bank, was on track.

cases.conditions: Reuters reported that the regulator raised business prices and ended the cheaper household tier to help power companies pay off debt and meet criteria set by international lenders; households moved from 7.7 lek per kWh under 300 kWh and 13.5 lek above it to a single 9.5 lek from 26 December 2014. Distributor OSHEE had to cut unpaid debt from 48% of billed electricity to 22% in 2015. The IMF called for better collections and less theft, without naming prison terms. The government drafted the prison penalties in March 2014 (Top Channel); no source found shows they were a loan condition.
cases.community: A late-2014 reform made collecting household and business debts compulsory and made electricity theft punishable by prison (Tirana Times). Households repaying old debts paid 2,800 lek (€22) a month on top of normal use; pensioners and people on assistance paid 1,200 lek. At the end of March 2018, 54,200 consumers were still paying in instalments. A World Bank report cited by Tirana Times said almost half the population spent over 10% of income on energy. An unemployed man in Berat, Ilirjan Berati, was sentenced to 4 months in prison for non-payment, reduced to reporting weekly for 18 months (Citizens Channel). In 2019 about 3,200 people signed a petition from Roma and Egyptian activists asking for the relief for poor families promised in the 2015 law, which had not been approved.
cases.outcome: OSHEE reported grid losses down from 50% in early 2013 to about 28% in early 2018, and about 346,000 debtors paid in one sum. Bad debt of about 47.8 billion lek remained (Tirana Times).

companies.name: Inter RAO
companies.role: Russian state-owned electricity company that bought Electric Networks of Armenia in 2006 and owned it when the rise was approved and the protests took place

cases.suppression: On 23 June 2015 riot police used water cannon on protesters on Baghramyan Avenue. Police reported 237 arrests (Amnesty International; The Moscow Times says about 200). About 25 people went to hospital (PONARS Eurasia); police said seven protesters and 11 officers were hurt, none seriously (Amnesty). Amnesty reported journalists were targeted and equipment seized, and an eyewitness said plainclothes police beat peaceful protesters.
cases.title: Electric Yerevan: Protests at the Inter RAO Grid's Price Rise
cases.point: Baghramyan Avenue near the presidential palace, where police used water cannon on 23 June 2015
cases.conditions: No loan condition. The Russian-owned distributor said the fall of the dram made a rise necessary, and the state regulator approved it in June 2015, to apply from 1 August (Moscow Times).
cases.community: Bills were to rise by about 1.5 US cents per kWh from 1 August 2015 (PONARS Eurasia), reported as 17% (Hromadske) or 22% (Moscow Times). President Sargsyan said the government would cover the extra cost until an audit reported (Moscow Times). New owner Samvel Karapetyan offered to cover the difference for households and small businesses up to 250 kWh until 1 August 2016 (Hetq), and Jamestown reports the state budget also bore part of it.
cases.outcome: Police put one rally at 6,000 people (Moscow Times). Inter RAO sold the distributor to Tashir Group, with the price not disclosed (The Bulletin). In October 2015 the Prime Minister said Deloitte's audit found the rates justified (Hetq). JAMnews wrote in 2017 that the intended rise did not take place.

The detentions were by Armenian police, not the company; the tie is that the protests were against the rise sought by its foreign owner. Households were largely shielded from the rise, so the harm is the arrests and injuries, not higher bills. The rise is given as 17% or 22%. The government's audit found it justified; the sale price was not disclosed, and Jamestown says the state budget carried part of the cover.

cases.title: Jordan's Takaful Cash Aid Algorithm
cases.point: Amman, where Human Rights Watch interviewed applicants (the programme is national)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Two loans in 2018 and 2019 totalling US$2 billion backed reforms under IMF programmes, with US$200 million earmarked for social assistance; the US$1,014 million Emergency Cash Transfer COVID-19 Response Project was approved in June 2020 (HRW).

cases.conditions: HRW reports that the reforms backed by these loans removed fuel subsidies, raised sales tax, lowered the income tax threshold and restructured electricity tariffs. Cash aid was targeted through a formula rather than paid to all. HRW calls this the World Bank's push to allocate cash by algorithm.
cases.community: Human Rights Watch held 70 interviews, 36 of them with people or families who had applied. A woman in al-Burbaita, Tafilah, said her family received Takaful in 2021 and was dropped in 2022; she blames the car they use to haul water: 'The car destroyed us.' An Amman tailor supported in 2019 was cut off the next year, took 12,000 dinars in loans during Covid and thinks his shop counted against him. A Jordanian woman with a Syrian husband and three children was found ineligible for later rounds; she says a staff member told her 'your children are non-Jordanian, so we give you once and that's enough.' The National Aid Fund scores families on 57 indicators and counts only Jordanian household members; a car under five years old or a business worth 3,000 dinars means refusal. In the first half of 2022 over 400,000 households applied for 120,000 places. The Ministry of Planning reported poverty at 24.1% in the first quarter of 2022, against 15.7% recorded in 2018 (HRW).
cases.outcome: HRW asked Jordan and the Bank to publish the formula and move to universal social protection. The government declined to give the full list of indicators or their weights. The Bank said it was working with the Fund to refine the algorithm.

sources.title: Automated Neglect: How the World Bank's Push to Allocate Cash Assistance Using Algorithms Threatens Rights
World Bank/Jordan: Poverty Targeting Algorithms Harm Rights

cases.confidence_note: The refusals are applicants' accounts to Human Rights Watch, which says people go hungry, fall behind on rent and take on debt. Applicants infer why they were refused, since the formula is not public. No error rate is published, so how many eligible families were wrongly refused is unknown; the IMF noted that demand outstrips coverage. The World Bank calls Takaful among the most redistributive and cost-effective poverty programmes in Jordan. The National Aid Fund says older cars lower a family's ranking but do not disqualify it, and that no single indicator excludes a household.

lvwhy.cuts: Aid limited to a scored minority of applicants.
lvwhy.prices: HRW links the loans to reforms that removed fuel subsidies.
lvwhy.project: World Bank project pays the transfers through the targeted system.

cases.title: Kenya September 2018 Fuel VAT
cases.point: Nairobi, where fuel stations ran dry during the transporters' strike (the tax was national)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: US$1.5 billion precautionary stand-by approved 14 March 2016 for 24 months, suspended in mid-2017 after missed deficit targets, extended six months in March 2018 and ended on 14 September 2018 (The Star, The EastAfrican). Daily Nation and The Standard call the fuel tax an IMF condition; The Standard gave the facility as Sh150 billion.

cases.conditions: Treasury Principal Secretary Kamau Thugge said in March 2018 that the 16% VAT on petroleum products from September was in line with a deal Kenya made with the IMF two years earlier (Business Daily). The EastAfrican lists fuel VAT changes among the conditions Kenya had promised to meet. MPs moved to delay the tax by two years, but it took effect on 1 September 2018 (Daily Nation).
cases.community: Nairobi petrol reached Sh127 a litre and diesel Sh111.78; petrol in Mandera reached Sh141.61 (Daily Nation). The Treasury expected the tax to add up to Sh17 a litre (Business Daily). Bus and matatu owners in the Mt Kenya region announced a 20% fare rise from 1 September to cover the fuel cost (Business Daily). Petroleum transporters struck over the tax, and by the third day many stations were dry, with long queues where fuel remained (Business Daily).
cases.outcome: President Kenyatta defended the tax but proposed halving it to 8%, along with spending cuts (Africanews). Parliament's support for halving it was reported on 21 September (Green Fiscal Policy Network). The Motorists Association called fuel boycotts (Kenyans.co.ke).

cases.confidence_note: The tie to the IMF is stated by the Treasury's Principal Secretary and by Kenyan press; The Standard noted the government had not publicly confirmed the conditions it listed, and no IMF document was read. The tax rests on Kenya's own VAT Act of 2013 and Finance Act 2016 (Kenyans.co.ke). The IMF facility was suspended from mid-2017 and ended two weeks after the tax began. The harm shown is higher prices and fares and fuel shortages; no count of households who lost income was found.

cases.title: Sri Lanka 2024 VAT Rise to 18%
cases.point: Negombo, where parents and priests began a signature campaign on 22 February 2025 (the tax is national)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: US$3 billion Extended Fund Facility; the second payment of about US$330 million depended on prior actions, including revenue targets (Daily Mirror). AFP says taxes were raised to meet the bailout's conditions.

cases.conditions: Cabinet spokesman Bandula Gunawardana said the second IMF payment had not come 'because we couldn't meet the revenue targets set by the IMF', when announcing the VAT rise. The agreed target was revenue of 12% of GDP by 2024.
cases.community: From 1 January 2024 VAT rose from 15% to 18%, and 97 exempt goods and services, including fuel and gas, became taxed (Daily FT). Joseph Stalin of the Ceylon Teachers' Union said the VAT rise pushed up the price of exercise books; South China Morning Post reports that schools in poorer areas saw a significant drop in attendance, citing costs of supplies and transport. In Negombo in 2025 a mother told UCA News she paid about 13,000 rupees a term for books, up from 7,000 in 2023. Another said many families bought only half the required supplies and some children stopped attending.
cases.outcome: In February 2025 Catholic priests and activists began a national petition saying the new government had broken its promise to remove VAT on essentials (UCA News).

sources.title: Govt. to raise VAT to 18% to meet IMF revenue targets

cases.confidence_note: The tie to the IMF comes from the government's own spokesman and AFP. No IMF document was read. The school costs and attendance are parents', teachers' and schools' accounts, with no national count, and they also reflect other price rises. UCA News places the rise in the latest budget, though it took effect in January 2024.

lvwhy.tax: VAT raised to 18% and exemptions removed to meet IMF revenue targets.
lvwhy.prices: Costs of food, fuel and school supplies rose.

sources_add.title: Egypt raises fuel prices in fifth and final hike
Egypt raises fuel prices by up to 23%

extend.note: Adds the last step of the same IMF loan. On 5 July 2019, 92-octane petrol went from 6.75 to 8 pounds a litre, 80-octane and diesel from 5.50 to 6.75, and a cooking gas cylinder from 50 to 65 pounds; Ahram/AFP calls it the fifth and final petrol rise and a condition of the US$12 billion loan, with the last US$2 billion pending. Enerdata gives the cylinder as 100 to 130 pounds, also 30%, and says lower-voltage electricity users faced about 19% more from 1 July. The 2015-2018 poverty figures already on this case predate this rise and should not be read as its effect.

sources_add.title: Gas price for households in Ukraine grows by almost quarter Nov 1
Expensive gas for Ukrainians: IMF and elections in the background

extend.note: Adds the next step. From 1 November 2018 the household price rose 23.5%, from 6,958 to about 8,550 hryvnias per 1,000 cubic metres, while the IMF pressed for import parity, about a 30% rise (UNIAN). Describing its negotiations with the IMF, the government said partners required equal industrial and household gas prices, which meant 60% more for heating, and that it agreed 23%. The Warsaw Institute says a US$3.9 billion IMF programme came in return. 6.9 million households got gas subsidies that year and the 2019 budget set aside 55 billion hryvnias; the government said poorer homes would be covered. No count of households falling behind was found.
